Unacylated Ghrelin does not Acutely Affect Substrate Metabolism or Insulin 
Sensitivity in Men with Type 2 Diabetes

Objective  
Unacylated ghrelin (UAG) is suggested to improve insulin sensitivity with a therapeutic 
potential. We therefore tested the effects of intravenous UAG infusion on glucose and lipid 
metabolism, insulin sensitivity, and energy expenditure in men with type 2 diabetes (T2DM). 
Design 
A randomized double blind and placebo-controlled crossover study performed at a university 
hospital clinical research center. 
Methods 
Ten men with T2DM completed two study days: I) 6-h UAG (1 microgram/kg/h) infusion and II) 
6-h placebo (PL) infusion. The patients were investigated in the basal postabsorptive state for 4 
hours followed by a hyperinsulinemic clamp for 2 hours. The turnover rates of glucose and fatty 
acids were assayed by isotope tracer techniques. Energy expenditure was measured by indirect 
calorimetry. 
Results 
Plasma UAG was 64.1 ± 11.3 pg/ml at baseline and increased more than 50-fold during UAG 
infusion. Plasma glucose was 7.0 ± 0.3 [UAG] vs. 6.7 ± 0.4 [PL] mmol/l (P = 0.43) at baseline

and was not affected by UAG. During the hyperinsulinemic clamp, glucose infusion rates were 
4.69 ± 0.56 [UAG] vs. 4.98 ± 0.43 [PL] mg/kg/min (P = 0.66). UAG did not affect either glucose 
oxidation, non-oxidative glucose disposal, lipolysis, energy expenditure, or respiratory exchange 
rate. 
Conclusions 
This study demonstrates that native UAG exposure does not exert acute metabolic effects in men 
with T2DM.  
Precis: This study shows that intravenous infusion of unacylated ghrelin for 6 hrs. does not affect plasma 
glucose, insulin sensitivity, lipolysis, or energy expenditure in men with type 2 diabetes. 
Introduction 
Ghrelin is the endogenous ligand for the growth hormone (GH) secretagogue receptor (GHS-R) 
(1) and ghrelin infusion stimulates the release of both GH and adrenocorticotropic hormone 
(ACTH) (2), the latter of which translates into increased cortisol secretion (3). Hyperglycemia 
and lipolysis after ghrelin administration in healthy subjects is therefore partly mediated by GH 
and cortisol (3,4). The GHS-R is also present in skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, and liver (5,6) 
suggesting that ghrelin exerts direct tissue effects, and it was recently demonstrated that ghrelin 
induces insulin resistance and lipolysis independently of GH and cortisol (7). 
The ability of ghrelin to bind to the GHS-R depends on the presence of an acyl side chain 
attached to the serine-3 residue of the ghrelin molecule (1). The peptide known as unacylated 
ghrelin (UAG) is both a precursor to ghrelin and one of the split products, when ghrelin is 
deacylated during its degradation (1,8). 
Ghrelin and UAG are present in the circulation with a ratio between 1:3 (9) and 1:1 (8) 
depending on the assay technique. Although UAG does not bind to the GHS-R, it is proposed 
that UAG exerts metabolic effects partly by antagonizing ghrelin. As an example, co-
administration of UAG abolishes ghrelin-induced hyperglycemia in healthy controls (10) and 
prevents against insulin resistance after ghrelin exposure in GH-deficient patients (11). Some 
investigations also point toward direct metabolic effects of native UAG as it dose-dependently 
suppresses glucose output in porcine hepatocytes (12) and lowers postprandial and fasting 
plasma glucose and serum FFAs in healthy subjects (13). In patients with type 2 diabetes 
(T2DM), a recent study demonstrated that UAG infusion improved insulin sensitivity (14). 
In this randomized, double blind and placebo controlled crossover study, we therefore 
investigated metabolic effects of UAG in patients with T2DM using a hyperinsulinemic 
euglycemic clamp in combination with glucose and fatty acid tracer techniques and indirect 
calorimetry.  
Research Design and Methods 
This study was conducted in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration and all subjects gave their 
oral and written informed consent to participate. The local Ethics Committee and the Danish 
Medicines Agency approved the study protocol and the protocol was registered at EudraCT 
number 2013-000022-63 before the onset of enrolment. 
Preparation of study medication 
Synthetic human unacylated ghrelin (CS Bio Company, Menlo Park, CA) was dissolved in 
sterile water and passed through a 0.2 µm anti-bacterial filter and reconstituted in normal (0.9%) 
saline immediate prior to infusion. Normal saline was used as placebo and both study

medications were blinded to the patients and the study personnel. The infusion solutions were 
prepared by the hospital pharmaceutical services and complied with GMP, GDP, and GCP 
guidelines. 
Subjects 
Ten men with T2DM (age 52.4 ± 1.8 years, BMI 30.1 ± 1.3 kg/m2) participated (Table 1). None 
received insulin treatment. T2DM was diagnosed according to the criteria: Fasting plasma 
glucose (PG) >7.0 mM, HbA1C ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol), or 2-hour postprandial PG ≥ 11.1 mM 
(15). 
Study protocol 
The study was a randomized double blind and placebo-controlled crossover study and followed 
GCP guidelines. Each subject reported to our research facilities at 0800 hr. in the morning after 
an overnight fast. The patients emptied their urinary bladder before starting the metabolic study 
day. One i.v. cannula was inserted into an antecubital region for infusion, and one i.v. cannula 
was positioned in a dorsal hand vein for blood sampling. The hand was wrapped in a heat pad in 
order to arterialize the venous blood samples. The patients were investigated in the morning after 
an overnight fast in the supine position during a basal period of 4 hours followed by a primed 
continuous hyperinsulinemic clamp (insulin 1.0 mU/kg/min i.v., Actrapid, Novo Nordisk, 
Gentofte, Denmark) (HEC) for 2 hours on two separate occasions with: 1) intravenous UAG (1 
microgram/kg/h) and 2) placebo (PL) infusion, respectively. The studies were performed in a 
quiet, thermoneutral indoor environment and the patients were allowed oral water intake but no 
food during the trial. 
At t = 0 min, UAG or PL infusions and a primed (12 µCi) continuous (12 µCi/h) infusion of 
[3-3H] glucose were commenced. [9,10-3H]-palmitate was infused continuously at 0.3 µCi/min 
from 180 to 240 and from 300 to 360 min. 
During the insulin infusion, PG was clamped at ≈ 6.0 mmol/l by adjusting the rate of infusion 
of 20% glucose according to plasma glucose measurements carried out every 10 min. Serum 
insulin was measured at t = 270, 300, 330, and 360 min to document steady state. Insulin 
sensitivity, denoted the M value, was estimated by the  glucose infusion rate (GIR) during the 
terminal 30 min of the HEC. Glucose rate of disappearance (Rd) and palmitate flux were 
measured during the terminal 30 minutes of both the basal and the HEC using tracer dilution 
techniques. Indirect calorimetry was also performed during the terminal 30 minutes of both the 
basal and the HEC to measure energy expenditure (EE) and the respiratory exchange rate (RER). 
Additional blood samples were drawn as indicated in Figures 1 and 2 and analyzed for ghrelin 
(acyl), UAG, GH, cortisol, insulin, C-peptide, glucagon, and FFA. 
The patients urinated at t = 240 and 360 min and the urine was measured by volume and a 
sample was stored at -20 °C for later urea analysis. 
Biochemical analyses 
Plasma glucose was analyzed bedside using the glucose oxidase method (YSI 2300 STAT Plus; 
YSI Life Sciences, Yellow Springs, OH). Serum and plasma samples were frozen and stored at -
20 °C or at -80 °C (ghrelin, UAG, and glucagon). Serum FFAs were analyzed by a commercial 
kit (Wako Chemicals, Neuss, Germany). Samples for plasma ghrelin and UAG measurements 
were drawn in 2 ml acidified EDTA prepared vacutainers with 20 µl 200 mg/ml AEBSF (Sigma-
Aldrich Denmark A/S, Copenhagen, Denmark) and centrifuged immediately at 2,500 g for 10 
minutes at 4°C. The serine protease inhibitor AEBSF was added to the collecting blood tubes to 
reduce breakdown of acyl ghrelin. Plasma was then transferred to 1.8 ml tubes and stored at -80

°C until analysis. Plasma ghrelin and UAG were measured by ELISAs (Bertin Pharma, 
Montigny-le-Bretonneux, France; A05106 and A05119, respectively) using a modified protocol 
(16). Serum GH was analyzed using chemiluminescence technology (IDS-iSYS Multi-Discipline 
Automated Analyzer, Immunodiagnostic Systems Nordic a/s Herlev, Denmark). Serum insulin 
was analyzed using time-resolved fluoroimmunoassay assay (AutoDELFIA Insulin kit, catalog 
no. B080–101, PerkinElmer, Turku, Finland). Serum cortisol was measured using a DRG ELISA 
kit (DRG Instruments GmbH, Marburg, Germany). Plasma glucagon was measured by an in-
house radioimmuno assay modified from (17). The specific activity of [3-3H] glucose was 
determined as previously described (18). Rates of glucose appearance (Ra) and Rd were 
calculated using Steele’s non-steady state equation using a pool fraction of 0.65. Endogenous 
glucose production (EGP) during the HEC, which is a measure of hepatic insulin sensitivity, was 
calculated by subtracting the glucose infusion rate from glucose Ra during the terminal 30 min of 
the HEC. For palmitate, blood samples were drawn for analysis of palmitate concentration and 
specific activity (SA). Steady state of SA was verified (t = 210 to 240 and 330 to 360 min) for 
each individual. Plasma palmitate concentration and SA were determined by HPLC using [2H31]-
palmitate as internal standard. Systemic palmitate flux (rate of appearance, µmol/min) was 
calculated using the [9,10-3H]-palmitate infusion rate (dpm/min) divided by the steady state 
palmitate SA (dpm/µmol). EE and RER were calculated by indirect calorimetry using a 
computerized open circuit system (Oxycon Pro; Intramedic, Gentofte, Denmark). Oxidation rates 
of glucose (GOX) and lipids were calculated from EE and RER after correction for protein 
oxidation, which was estimated from the urinary excretion of urea. Nonoxidative glucose 
disposal (NOGD) was calculated as whole body Rd minus the rate of GOX (19). 
Statistical analysis 
Results are expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (mean ± SE) or median and 25 to 75 
percentiles if data was non-normal distributed. SigmaPlot 11.0 (©Systat Software, CA) was used 
for the statistical analyses. Mean concentrations were used to test for significant differences in 
time series and the GIR. Concentrations at single time points were analyzed by a Student’s two-
tailed paired t test or a Signed Rank Test in non-normal distributed data. A P value < 0.05 was 
considered significant. 
Results 
Hormones 
The hormone concentrations are depicted in Figure 1. Plasma UAG concentrations were 64.1 ± 
11.3 pg/ml at baseline and increased by a factor > 50 reaching a plateau after 240 minutes. The 
ghrelin to UAG ratio was 1.4:1 at baseline and decreased successively to 0.018:1. The following 
circulating hormonal concentrations were similar at baseline: ghrelin (pg/ml) [42.6 (24.5 – 
123.5) [UAG] vs. 38.3 (25.8 – 76.6) [PL] (P = 0.82)]; insulin (pmol/l) [65.0 ± 15.1 [UAG] vs. 
64.3 ± 13.2 [PL] (P = 0.86)]; C-peptide (pmol/l) [512.0 ± 80.9 [UAG] vs. 515.4 ± 81.7 [PL] (P = 
0.93)]; GH (ng/ml) [0.07 (0 – 0.12) [UAG] vs. 0.08 (0.06 – 0.13) [PL] (P = 0.46)]; cortisol 
(ng/ml) [127.6 ± 119 [UAG] vs. 146.0 ± 18.7 [PL] (P = 0.20)]; and glucagon (ng/ml) [72.7 ± 8.0 
[UAG] vs. 72.5 ± 8.2 [PL] (P = 0.97)].  
Metabolites 
Plasma glucose and FFA levels are depicted in Figure 2. Fasting PG was similar at baseline 
(mmol/l) [7.0 ± 0.3 [UAG] vs. 6.7 ± 0.4 [PL] (P = 0.43)]. UAG infusion had no effect on PG 
levels, as PG decreased equally in both interventions during the basal period to similar nadir

levels at t = 240 min (mmol/l) [6.3 ± 0.2 [UAG] vs. 6.1 ± 0.3 [PL] (P = 0.25)]. During the HEC, 
PG was clamped at similar levels (mmol/l) [6.2 ± 0.1 [UAG] vs. 6.1 ± 0.0 [PL] (P = 0.29)]. 
FFAs at baseline were similar (mmol/l) [0.46 ± 0.06 [UAG] vs. 0.52 ± 0.03 [PL] (P = 0.47)], 
and remained at similar levels during both interventions in the basal period (mmol/l) [0.48 ± 0.05 
[UAG] vs. 0.49 ± 0.04 [PL] (P = 0.90)], and decreased to the same extent during the HEC 
(mmol/l) [0.07 ± 0.01 [UAG] vs. 0.07 ± 0.02 [PL] (P = 0.99)]. 
Glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity 
The GIR during the HEC is depicted in Figure 3. UAG infusion did not improve peripheral 
insulin sensitivity as assessed by the M value (in mg glucose/kg/min) [4.69 ± 0.56 [UAG] vs. 
4.98 ± 0.43 [PL] (P = 0.66)]. Hepatic insulin sensitivity, as determined by EGP, was also not 
affected by UAG in basal period (in mg glucose/kg/min) [1.48 ± 0.09 [UAG] vs. 1.35 ± 0.12 
[PL] (P = 0.31)] or in the HEC [0.75 ± 0.13 [UAG] vs. 0.57 ± 0.40 [PL] (P = 0.70)], Figure 3C. 
Glucose disposal is shown in Figure 3D. UAG did not significantly affect glucose turnover 
during the basal period (in mg glucose/kg/min) [1.68 ± 0.11 [UAG] vs. 1.57 ± 0.12 [PL] (P = 
0.38)] or during the HEC [4.10 ± 0.46 [UAG] vs. 3.97 ± 0.51 [PL] (P = 0.85)]. Both oxidative 
glucose disposal (GOX) and non-oxidative glucose disposal (NOGD) were similar during UAG 
and PL. GOX in the basal period (in mg glucose/kg/min) [1.19 ± 0.16 [UAG] vs. 0.94 ± 0.15 
[PL] (P = 0.27)]; GOX in the HEC [1.68 ± 0.20 [UAG] vs. 1.70 ± 0.11 [PL] (P = 0.94)]; NOGD 
in the basal period (in mg glucose/kg/min) [0.50 ± 0.15 [UAG] vs. 0.63 ± 0.18 [PL] (P = 0.60)]; 
NOGD in the HEC [2.43 ± 0.47 [UAG] vs. 2.32 ± 0.57 [PL] (P = 0.88)]. 
Lipid metabolism 
Palmitate fluxes are depicted in Figure 4A. Systemic palmitate fluxes were similar in the basal 
period (µmoles/min) [215.2 ± 26.3 [UAG] vs. 223.7 ± 26.2 [PL] (P = 0.78)] and in the HEC, 
where they were suppressed to a similar extent [58.0 ± 7.9 [UAG] vs. 55.2 ± 6.6 [PL] (P = 
0.68)]. 
Energy expenditure and the respiratory exchange rate 
Data from indirect calorimetry are depicted in Figure 4B and C. UAG infusion did not impact on 
EE in the basal period (kcal/24 hrs.) [1773 ± 95 [UAG] vs. 1802 ± 69 [PL] (P = 0.61)] or in the 
HEC [1722 ± 89 [UAG] vs. 1818 ± 77 [PL] (P = 0.29)], or on RER in the basal period [0.83 ± 
0.01 [UAG] vs. 0.82 ± 0.01 [PL] (P = 0.40) or in the HEC [0.86 ± 0.01 [UAG] vs. 0.87 ± 0.02 
[PL] (P = 0.53)]. 
No side effects were observed. 
Discussion 
The data from the present study show that short-term intravenous UAG infusion does not affect 
either substrate metabolism or insulin sensitivity in men with T2DM. These findings are 
important for the following reasons. First, the high prevalence of T2DM mandates novel and 
improved treatment methods. Second, a number of reports suggest UAG as a potential anti-
diabetic drug, and several clinical trials on the effect of UAG in T2DM are ongoing (20-22).  
Failure to detect any significant effect on UAG has previously been reported by Tong et al. in 
a short-term 2 x 2 factorial design with ghrelin, UAG, and placebo, where healthy subjects were 
studied with the following endpoints: The acute insulin response to intravenous glucose infusion, 
insulin sensitivity index, disposition index, and intravenous glucose tolerance. None of the 
metabolic endpoints were affected by UAG in their study (23).

Several clinical, rodent, and in vitro cell studies have, however, demonstrated that UAG 
exerts positive metabolic effects on substrate metabolism (20). It is suggested that UAG acts as a 
functional antagonist to ghrelin, which directly induces lipolysis and insulin resistance in skeletal 
muscle (7,24), and reduces ghrelin levels in addition to possessing specific ghrelin-independent 
endocrine and metabolic effects (20). Insulin resistance is associated with relative UAG 
deficiency (25,26), which has led to the hypothesis that interventions that increase the UAG to 
ghrelin ratio could improve insulin action. In clinical experiments, the UAG to ghrelin ratio was 
affected by UAG administration, and UAG treatment in healthy subjects counteracted the 
hyperglycemic and insulin lowering effects of ghrelin (10), and in patients with GH-deficiency, 
UAG prevented ghrelin-induced lipolysis and insulin resistance (11). It has also been observed 
that total (11) and acyl ghrelin (14) concentrations decrease after UAG administration. 
Due to the design of our study, we cannot rule out a putative ghrelin-antagonistic effect of 
UAG, which would have demanded a 2 x 2 factorial design with ghrelin and UAG. In insulin 
resistant obese subjects, AG correlate positively and UAG inversely with insulin resistance (25), 
which suggests that a relative AG surplus combined with a relative UAG deficiency may play a 
role in decreased insulin sensitivity.    
We did not observe an effect of UAG on ghrelin levels or on hyperglycemia and insulin 
concentrations, but it is not possible to directly compare our data to others, since the UAG 
infusion rate in the study by Özcan et al. (14) was 10 fold higher as compared to ours. 
Our results do not support that short term UAG exposure elicits either ghrelin-dependent or 
direct effects, but higher UAG concentrations and more prolonged UAG exposition may be 
required to detect an effect. Indeed, Delhanty et al. demonstrated metabolically favorable 
changes in gene expressions after 6 hours of UAG exposure in ghsr-/- mice (27). Putative 
biological effects of changes in gene expression may therefore be detected only after more than 6 
hours, although the exact period remains to be examined. 
Some additional limitations apply to our study. Our study cohort was relatively small, and 
included men only. The study subjects had a BMI mostly in the overweight range and a 
relatively well controlled T2DM with low or even normal HbA1c levels and some of the patients 
were relatively insulin sensitive with an M value in the normal range (28). These limitations 
precludes us from extrapolating our data to women with diabetes and to patients with less 
efficient diabetes control. Moreover, we did not measure oral glucose tolerance, which is 
noteworthy since UAG has been suggested to act as an insulin sensitizer (14,21,22). 
In conclusion, our data show that UAG infusion to men with T2DM does not affect basal or 
insulin stimulated substrate metabolism or insulin sensitivity. Studies on long-term effects of 
UAG or its analogs on glucose and lipid metabolism remain to be conducted to determine if 
modulation of the ghrelin system could play a role in future diabetes treatment.
